utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The purpose of today's hearing is to learn more about the current work of the New York City Department of Sanitation and the Business Integrity Commission to seek value from our discarded materials and to help further the circular economy in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez

chapters.summary: DSNY Commissioner Gregory Anderson introduces his team and traces the history of recycling in NYC from 19th-century rag pickers through Local Law 19 of 1989, describing the evolution from take-make-waste to modern recycling and composting programs.
chapters.title: Commissioner Anderson gives historical overview of NYC recycling and waste management

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez and members of the Committee on Sanitation and Solid Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm Gregory Anderson, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Jennifer McDonald, Deputy Commissioner of Solid Waste Management, Kate Kitchener, Executive Director of Resource Recovery at DSNY, and Jane Gajwani, Director of the Office of Energy and Resource Recovery at DEP.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Thank you for inviting us to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll start with a little history.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: New Yorkers have been recycling in some form for more than 200 years.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In the 19th century, rendering plants, scrap dealers, and an informal network of rag and bone pickers ensured that the most usable discards were given new life.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In the early 20th century, during the World Wars and the Great Depression, New Yorkers used and reused products out of a sense of civic duty, necessity, or both.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But in the 20th century, industrial growth and economic transformation in the United States built a powerful economy.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Based on the insatiable appetite of a growing population of Americans as consumers of products, of energy, of land, and of water.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The fundamental premise of this 20th century economy was to take, make, and waste both natural and labor resources from around the globe to fuel economic growth.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: At the same time, we found every possible way to dispose of the growing volumes of trash we generated, dump it in the ocean, burn it, bury it in giant mountains of trash.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And over time, there was a growing realization that we are asking more of our planet and of its people than we can endure, and that this economic model, take-make-waste, was unsustainable.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And here in New York City, we struggled with the reality that our means of disposal in polluting incinerators, in barely regulated landfills across the city, and the behemoth Fresh Kills landfill on Staten Island would not last.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: For decades, the Department of Sanitation has endeavored to recover and reclaim as much of the value remaining in the products New Yorkers use, whether by reuse, recycling, or composting, through conversion to energy, or through other means.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Now, our modern recycling programs were born out of the environmental movement of the 1970s and 80s, beginning with grassroots efforts to collect recyclable products like cans and newspapers at the neighborhood level.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: New York City instituted its first recycling program in 85, collecting old newspapers in Greenwich Village before expanding to other neighborhoods and other material types.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Local Law 19 of 1989 codified the city's mandatory curbside recycling program and is the foundation of the city's recycling program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: of the program we have today.

chapters.summary: Anderson describes DSNY's 24-million-pound daily collection, public-private partnerships like the Staten Island Compost Facility and Sunset Park Materials Recovery Facility, and the forthcoming 2026 Solid Waste Management Plan (SWAMP) guiding future resource recovery.
chapters.title: Anderson discusses 2026 Solid Waste Management Plan and current diversion efforts

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: More recently, we've created the largest mandatory curbside composting program in the nation to collect compostable material, food scraps, yard waste, food soil, paper,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: so we can turn it into finished compost or into renewable energy, far, far better than shipping it to landfills hundreds of miles away.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As we continue our work to create a more circular economy, we are in the process of finalizing our 2026 Solid Waste Management Plan, or SWAMP for short, a 10-year plan designed to guide the future of resource recovery in our city.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We remain on track to complete the plan this year, and we look forward to continued engagement with the City Council regarding its completion and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Sanitation collects and processes 24 million pounds of trash, recycling, and compost, and compostable material, every day.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And for many decades, one of our goals has been to put as much of this material to beneficial reuse as possible.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: What items can achieve beneficial use, though, changes with technological development and with the shifting markets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are also formal and informal exchanges of used and unwanted goods in thrift stores, on WhatsApp chats, and at stoops that ensure that products with value stay in circulation well beyond just one initial use.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: In our experience at DSNY, recovering value from waste has worked best when the public sector and private sector come together to make investments in sustainable processes and facilities to support waste diversion.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The Staten Island Compost Facility was built by the City of New York, and much of its operation is handled by a private contractor.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We process millions of pounds of food waste and yard waste there every year, keeping that material out of landfills and producing valuable compost, which we both sell and give away to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Likewise, the Sunset Park Materials Recovery Facility is built on city land, which was improved with city capital funds, but the facility itself was built and is operated by a private sector partner.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And nowhere is the value of these public-private investments in the circular economy clearer than at the Pratt Industries paper mill on Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Thanks to tens of millions in private and public investment, when you throw away a newspaper or a cardboard box in your green recycling bin in Manhattan today,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: it will be barged to Staten Island to become a pizza box sold potentially in Brooklyn next week.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that's recycling at work.

chapters.summary: Anderson highlights textiles as 5% of the waste stream, current drop-off programs, and interest in private-sector mass-market solutions. He also discusses lithium battery disposal dangers and the need for producer responsibility to keep sanitation workers safe.
chapters.title: Anderson addresses textile recycling and lithium battery challenges

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Similar model may be the path forward for two of our biggest challenges in the development of our waste management infrastructure, for used textiles and for lithium batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: For textiles, which represent about 5% of New York City's waste stream, there are a number of not-for-profit and for-profit entities developing their own operational capacity for sorting and processing, and DSNY is ready to assist as this industry develops.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Our current textile recycling partnership provides easy, convenient drop-off for many New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But we are interested in working with private sector partners to develop mass market solutions more aligned with our composting and traditional recycling programs.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Lithium batteries, on the other hand, have suddenly appeared in an incredible variety of products.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that means they're in the trash somewhere in the city every single day.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They explode in our trucks and put sanitation workers and other workers at risk.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Imagine a world where lithium battery recycling becomes the economically preferable alternative to disposal, and producers are therefore incentivized to ensure proper handling of these items.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Shifting this response.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: responsibility of the private sector would keep sanitation workers safer and reduce the extractive impacts of lithium mining.

chapters.summary: Anderson advocates for EPR laws shifting recycling costs from taxpayers to manufacturers, noting NYC could receive over $100 million annually. He urges Albany to pass packaging EPR legislation and thanks the Council for prior support.
chapters.title: Anderson calls for extended producer responsibility and state packaging legislation

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As we look to the future, we're encouraged by efforts to create new partnerships to reduce waste, increase waste diversion, and move to a more circular economy.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have long supported the creation of extended producer responsibility laws to shift the financial and physical responsibility for recycling and disposing of products

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: from local governments like us and our taxpayers to the companies that manufacture, sell, and distribute these products to consumers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Chief among these is packaging waste, created explicitly for one-time use and often difficult to separate, sort, and remanufacture, leaving New York taxpayers holding the bill to collect and process these materials.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: An EPR program for packaging would incentivize manufacturers to reduce waste and increase recyclability

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and the use of recycled content, lowering recycling and disposal costs for cities, saving taxpayers money, and reducing the waste sent to landfills.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Based on bills previously introduced in the state legislature, New York City alone stands to receive more than $100 million annually to support our recycling program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: An investment in new infrastructure and consumer education.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I thank the Council for its prior support on this important issue, and I call on our partners in Albany to work with municipalities and recyclers across the state to get this bill across the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: line once and for all.

chapters.summary: Anderson expresses support for the intent of Intro 256 (textile recycling study) and describes current textile diversion programs. On Intro 970 (nightlife district cleaning), DSNY supports the intent and looks forward to discussing specific neighborhoods and resources needed.
chapters.title: Anderson states DSNY positions on Intro 256 and Intro 970

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation on today's agenda, Intro 256, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, would require DSNY to study the feasibility and potential environmental effects of a mandate for the source separation of textiles by households and the collection of these items by DSNY.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We support the intent of this bill to increase the amount of textiles diverted from landfills, which make up at least 5% of the city's

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: residential and institutional waste stream.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY currently offers several programs to divert textiles from landfills, including in-building collection for residential buildings with 10 or more units,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: as well as commercial buildings, schools, and nonprofits, community recycling events in all 59 community districts annually,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and publicly accessible textile collection bins in every borough.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing this bill further with the Council and discussing strategies to increase diversion of this material.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: On Intro 970, sponsored by Councilmember Gutierrez, which would require DSNY to designate nightlife districts and provide supplemental street cleaning and litter basket services in such districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: DSNY supports the intent of this legislation to keep neighborhoods clean, and we look forward to further conversations around the specific neighborhoods that would be covered by this bill and the resources that would be needed to provide this supplemental service.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So thank you again for the opportunity to testify today, and we look forward to answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Okay, so...

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY's waste categorization by product type remains effective and whether the agency is exploring new categorization methods. Anderson says the current approach works well because it aligns with remanufacturing markets and will be refined in the next waste characterization study.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on waste stream categorization effectiveness

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, so is the way that the department categorizes its waste streams, for example, metal, glass, plastic, textiles, and organics, still effective?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is the agency exploring new ways to categorize waste to facilitate sorting and other downstream disposal and recycling processes?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, we think that the categorization that we've used, which is generally based on product type, is very effective because at the end of the day, we are trying to produce materials for markets to remanufacture those products into new products.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So when we do our waste characterization study next year, for example, we will try to identify, you know, looking at the plastics, what kinds of plastics are in the waste stream.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then think about, you know, are there markets for those plastics?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Are we successfully, are New Yorkers successfully separating those products in their home?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Are we successfully sorting them at our material recovery facility?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And ultimately, are those getting turned into new products down the road?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we think it's successful, yes.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how DSNY prepares for new waste types like lithium-ion batteries. Anderson emphasizes that EPR for packaging would force companies to design for end-of-life, and notes DSNY is often reactive to new products but works with partners to identify emerging waste streams.
chapters.title: Sanchez and Anderson discuss preparing for new waste types from emerging technologies

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there also any conversation, given how rapidly technology is just moving and new products are coming around and, you know, lithium ion batteries were not a thing

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: 25 years ago, as we're experiencing all of these new technologies and these new kinds of waste, are we preparing or understanding what those...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: New things happening to our waste streams look like and how they're affecting our waste?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think this is where, for packaging in particular, where an EPR program would have a massive impact because it would require companies, as they're looking at new packaging products, to think about the end

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: use of those products and the

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: of those products, the recycled content that's contained within them.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think right now packaging companies are looking at a variety of other performance-related aspects of their packaging.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Does it keep food fresh, for example?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That is a good goal to have.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But if it keeps food fresh and can't be recycled, we need to be able to balance those two components to make sure that we are...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, designing packaging that works best, you know, for the entire life cycle of the value chain.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's what an EPR program would do for packaging in particular.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, there are always new products that are coming onto the market.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And unfortunately, because we're at the end of the line, we end up being very reactive around developing programs for those new products.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think rechargeable batteries are a great example there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, we're always working with our partners across the country and, you know, even around the world to try to identify those new things as they're coming up.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's almost like there's a bill in Albany that will help us be proactive about that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yes, Albany, I'm looking at you.

chapters.summary: Sanchez raises the challenge of limited space for composting. Anderson explains composting is space-intensive, DSNY supports community composters, and the best opportunity for industrial-scale composting is on Rikers Island as jails close.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on limited space for composting facilities

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: One challenge facing local composting efforts includes limited space for composting facilities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So how does the department plan to help address this problem?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, composting is a very space-intensive use.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's just the nature.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: of the business.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think, you know, we have for a long time worked with community composters and community gardens to give them the technical resources, the know-how, the tools to be able to compost, you know,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: where they're at in their community garden, in a neighborhood park, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Transitioning that to composting at scale is very challenging.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think one of the best opportunities we have, as we've discussed before, is the space on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As the jails on Rikers Island close, there will be a huge amount of space, and we would love to get a piece of that for industrial-scale composting and really to do so

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: in a way that is at the forefront of innovation and technology where potentially we could use a smaller footprint by taking advantage of new technologies that are on the market.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to make sure that people know we've been joined by Councilmember Inna Bernikoff.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about expanding food donation efforts, the Donate NYC portal, and food waste estimates from restaurants. Anderson says the Mayor's Office of Food Policy leads food rescue, the portal is not productive, and resources are better spent on capacity building for nonprofits. Kate Kitchener provides tonnage data.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on food donation and Donate NYC portal

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the department's goals for the draft swamp includes expanding food donation and other edible food recovery efforts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does the department plan to do that specifically?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It notes that it will work to increase the amount of food donated by businesses.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Have you already started that work, and what does that work entail specifically?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then does the department plan to expand the Donate NYC portal that already exists?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then how much food waste does the department currently estimate it collects from food service establishments?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I'll respond to those questions in order.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think first and foremost, we do a lot of work with the Mayor's Office of Food Policy, and they really lead the work around food rescue, food donation, and feeding hungry New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They convene all of the food recovery partners, everything from large organizations like City Harvest and Food Bank for New York City, down to neighborhood pantries or folks

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: doing work in their community.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: One of the steps that I think will be really helpful in this space is the additional language that the council added to the commercial organics law, which takes effects later this year, which requires commercial carters to provide information about food donation

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: to each of the businesses that they have that participates in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: compost collection, which will be mandatory for all businesses in New York City as of next year.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think that will really close the loop there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As far as the Donate NYC Food Portal, I think, to be frank, it's not a very productive use of our resources.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: This is a space where there are lots of organizations already operating really effectively.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And to ask government to come in and make these kinds of connections on a business-to-business level, I think really just is not super productive.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we haven't moved a lot of material through that portal since it was created, I don't know, probably seven or eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think probably where we are better suited to apply our resources is in capacity building for the nonprofits that are already operating in this space.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think one of the things that we hear from them is transportation and real estate are two of the biggest constraints that they have.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If we can, as a city, provide more resources to help solve some of those problems, I think they could probably achieve a lot more than we could through the food donation portal.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And then as far as numbers around food waste donated or rescued, I'll turn it over to Kate for this.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So I think there's two important numbers to look at here.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: There's the food portal that we have, and then there's also the Donate NYC program partners with food rescue networks across the city, as the commissioner has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And so for the food donations through the portal, you know, we've seen over the years,

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: You know, it's around, you know, it's kind of decreased.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: It started out strong, but we really only got one-time funding for that program.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And so in the recent years, you know, it's been around five tons a year.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: The partners, you know, which include places like City Harvest, those numbers are much bigger, right?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So we can really see what they're doing, you know, and that's closer to like around 40,000 tons a year.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So you can really see that like the partners are doing a great job.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And as the commissioner mentioned, we're working very closely with the mayor's office of food policy to

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: support those groups and what they're doing and we've actually been meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: We had a summit last fall with all the food rescue networks and then we've been had we have several meetings to try to address some of the challenges around technology, transportation and logistics as the commissioner mentioned and

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: you know, I think that's MOFP is really taking the lead there, but sanitation is happy to support.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And just generally, do you know how much actual food waste you're getting from restaurant establishments?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So that's, you mean like, so organics are collected by private haulers, not by sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Is that, I'm sorry, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: No, but if they're not like actually, you know, estimating how much food just actually goes to waste.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: That we don't, we don't have those numbers yet, but maybe as we see the commercial waste program roll out, we are hoping to get better data around that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez notes DSNY collected 187,000 tons of textile waste but diverted only 4.3%, asking about historical difficulties and program utilization. Anderson explains the in-building textile collection program has about 2,500 enrolled buildings, is voluntary, and faces challenges from informal reuse that can't be measured.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on textile recycling diversion rates and building participation

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And in fiscal year 25, the department collected 187,000 tons of textile waste, but only diverted 4.3%.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you explain the historical difficulties of textile recycling and diversion in the city?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Do you believe that the department-hosted textile drop-off sites, there's one in my building, thank you, and the free DSNY textile recycling collection program for in-building collection are being

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: successfully utilized by New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then how might the department encourage more buildings to participate in the...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Textile recycling program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So today we have around 2,500 buildings enrolled in our in-building textile collection program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think one of the important points of comparison here is between our in-building textile collection program and our in-building electronics collection program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Electronics disposal has been prohibited by state law for over a decade, and so participation in that program is much more robust.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Textile collection is totally voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's up to the building if they want to join.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We think it's a really great program because we give you the bin, you set it up in your building.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Whenever it's full, you call us and our partner comes to pick it up.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's a great, I think, additional amenity that buildings can offer their residents, but it is, again, totally voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's a space where there's certainly more opportunity for additional outreach, additional engagement to grow that program, which has been relatively stagnant for the last few years.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As far as the textile collection more generally, I think part of the challenge, and I sort of pointed at this in my testimony, is there's a lot of informal.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Uh,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: you know, reuse of material that's happening that we can't measure.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So the numbers that we look at in our waste characterization study really are only looking at the end of the line.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's material that actually ends up in the trash and how much of what would end up in the trash gets reused or recycled through programs that we run.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But, you know, I have a two-year-old.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I can tell you that the WhatsApp groups are, you know, they go crazy for kids'clothes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And whenever we, you know, whenever my daughter grows out of a size, we can always find someone to take that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But no one's measuring the probably hundreds of pounds of one's.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: and other things that I've donated over the years.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about business compliance with textile rules given businesses produce roughly 10% of textile waste. Anderson says DSNY lacks good data on commercial textile recovery but hopes a future commercial waste characterization study after commercial waste zones rollout will provide insights.
chapters.title: Sanchez and Anderson discuss business textile waste and commercial waste characterization

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm curious, so businesses produce roughly like 10% of the textile waste stream, and so how have you seen businesses comply with some of these rules?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think that's a space that we haven't done a lot of measurement in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There is, I would say, a pretty robust industry around the reuse of textiles, particularly from the fashion industry.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so I think that that exists, but we don't have great data on how much material is actually being recovered and how much material is ending up in the waste stream.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think this is a space where, you know, when we're able to do another,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: or not another, but really a first commercial waste characterization study at some point in the future after commercial waste zones is fully rolled out, we'll have a much better understanding of

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: how much textiles there are in the waste stream, where they're coming from, what the condition is at the time of disposal, and really be able to dive into programs around that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, this is an area that in the swamp, which we hope to finalize in the coming months, we have a number of initiatives around this specific topic.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about alternatives to rock salt for de-icing and new technologies beyond anaerobic digestion. Anderson says alternatives like CMA are 10-20x more expensive and not available at scale, and discusses pyrolysis as a proven technology for hard-to-recycle materials needing rigorous scientific analysis.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on rock salt alternatives and waste-to-energy technologies

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And a complete left field before I turn it over to some of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: The department uses a significant amount of rock.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: salts and brine to de-ice the streets.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has the department explored other alternatives to rock salts and brine like CMA?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And has the department researched other technologies in addition to anaerobic digestion or waste to energy that it can produce?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: That could improve the extraction of valuable materials from the city's waste streams?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we'll start with the salt question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And the short answer is yes, we have explored alternatives to rock salt last year, which was the heaviest winter we've had in quite some time.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We used about 505,000 tons.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Of salt, which is a significant amount.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I will say, you know, there are, there is a conversation in the, in the sort of roadway maintenance and public works industry around the use of rock salt for, you know,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: fighting snow and it's a much more pressing conversation in places like

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: you know near the Great Lakes near the Delaware River and other freshwater receiving waters particularly freshwater receiving waters that are sensitive environments or that are drinking water sources here in New York City we have

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: you know just a handful of freshwater

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: streams and creeks and the majority of our sewer system discharges into salt water.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So there isn't that same urgency around the

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: the impact of salt pollution on freshwater receiving waters.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But we do understand that there are implications for our infrastructure, particularly our transportation and energy infrastructure, and the corrosive impacts that road salt can have.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: When we've looked at alternatives, I think the challenge comes down to two things.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: One is effectiveness, the other is cost.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We've looked at some alternatives like the alternative brines and the beet sugar-based products that have been tested in the Midwest.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They're just simply not effective.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And for things like the calcium magnesium acetate, they can be effective, but being able to procure at the volume that we need, one, there isn't manufacturing capacity for those kinds of products at the volume that we would need.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And two, they are tremendously expensive, upwards of.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: 10 to 20 times more expensive per ton than road salt.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, I think that would be potentially prohibitive.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Oh, and sorry, other half of your question, anaerobic digestion.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Can you just restate the second half?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has the department researched other technologies in addition to anaerobic digestion or waste to energy that could improve the extraction of valuable materials from the city's waste streams?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so we certainly have.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think, you know, there's a whole dialogue in the industry right now around technologies to extract value from the waste stream.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Some of these technologies have unfortunately been treated like the boogeyman.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There are things like paralysis, which I think is a...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, maybe 10 years ago, was a relatively unproven technology at scale, but I think has really proven out its usefulness in certain contexts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It is not a one-size-fits-all solution, but for certain products that are difficult or nearly impossible to recycle through other means, it can be an effective solution to divert material from landfill.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think we need to do a much more rigorous sort of analysis of those kinds of technologies, you know, in a fair and scientific way instead of the much more emotional way that we've approached those technologies in the past.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how businesses are made aware of the textile recycling program. Kate Kitchener explains the program is primarily residential but DSNY does outreach to certain business types like laundromats.
chapters.title: Councilmember Thomas-Henry questions DSNY on textile program business awareness

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I will now pass the mic over to Councilmember Shanel Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I have two questions, one on topic, one off.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For the textile program, how are businesses being made aware that the program exists?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'll pass it over to Kate, who manages that program.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, so as we mentioned, the program is primarily for residential buildings, but we do allow commercial buildings to have a bin in their building.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And so we have staff that do outreach to certain business types that might be interested in having textiles, laundromats that might have a lost and found, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So that's how we get the word out around that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So it's predominantly for homeowners, not necessarily textile manufacturers or the like.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thanks for the clarity.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry raises rampant illegal dumping of mattresses and appliances in her district, asking about disposal sites and mitigation plans. Anderson explains DSNY no longer operates self-help sites, residential pickup is available 2-3 times weekly, and identifies a gap for small-scale construction waste disposal.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions Anderson on illegal dumping and disposal site gaps

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a question on dumping.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Currently, now originally I thought there were sites throughout the city where individuals can dump, but it seems like they're just special waste drop sites.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: They currently know.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So what is a rampant problem in my district is it seems as if individuals are cleaning out homes and then just dumping anything from mattresses, microwaves, and the like in areas.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is there any plan sanitation has in addition to the cameras to...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: mitigate this?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so in the, I would say, very distant past, probably before many of us were alive, the department did operate what were called self-help sites where homeowners could bring a load of whatever

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: trash they had and dispose of it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That was back when we operated the Fresh Kills landfill and we had transfer stations and landfills all across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We have not operated those self-help sites in over 20-something years.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I don't know that given the current sort of regulatory environment and the permitting framework that we operate in today, that we'd be able to

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: to open those up for the kinds of like large scale loads of material that, um, that are typically the cause of illegal dumping.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Uh, I think that, you know, the, the two things I would say here is one, we go to every residential property in New York city two or three times a week.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so there's no need to illegally dump material because we will come to you and we will pick it up.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: On the other hand, if you are a contractor or you're doing renovations and you're hiring someone to come in and do your kitchen or your bathroom, once that project starts,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: there is an obligation that that material be handled through the private carding industry and be collected by a BIC registered hauler and disposed of at a licensed transact.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I will say one of the things that we have identified as a potential gap as we've been thinking about your colleague Ty Hankerson's bill

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: around the proper disposal of construction and demolition waste is that it may not be super easy if you don't have, you know,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If you're renovating an office building or converting an office building to residential, for example, that's a big job.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You're hiring dozens or hundreds of loads of private carters to come in.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But if you're just getting, if you own a house and you're just getting your bathroom done, that amount of material may not be enough to...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, call up a truck and have them come and get it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so there's a gap in terms of our ability, in terms of the industry's ability and the regulatory framework's ability to sort of offer that service at that scale.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's something that as we consider that bill, which we're thankful that he introduced, that, you know, I think we need to look for ways to fill that gap.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry requests marketing materials for residents and small contractors on proper disposal methods. Anderson confirms DSNY has materials for both and offers to share them with her office.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry asks about public education materials for proper disposal

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are there any marketing materials or any just information for both?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So like if I'm a resident, I'm cleaning out my apartment, it's okay to leave your stuff.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Because I'm sure a lot of homeowners oftentimes don't want to leave all the trash out because they think they may get a fine.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Same with small contractors who aren't aware that there are carding companies to...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Pick up?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is there any type of information that we can share with constituents to say, hey, this is the proper way to do this?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, we have materials for both, and we'd be happy to share that with your office.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry raises litter concerns from her children and asks about fines and proactive anti-litter efforts. Anderson shares the frustration, emphasizes building community pride and ownership, and notes the Council reduced littering fines around 2019, expressing openness to increasing them.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions Anderson on litter enforcement and community pride

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I know I said two, but I have one more on behalf of my children.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Litter is out of control.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: My babies remind me constantly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And now that I'm a council member, say, Mommy, what are you going to do about this?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Just thinking back to when I was young, like, you knew not to throw trash on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like, it was just, and I believe there were fines.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Like, I don't even know if we have fines anymore.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are we doing anything proactively to encourage more New Yorkers to stop throwing their trash on the ground?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And even more specifically, as these rainstorms are coming, the drains are backing up.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: There's a lot of flooding, particularly in my district and other areas of Queens, because of trash.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think people today still know that they shouldn't throw things on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't think that that has changed.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I think it's because people, when you see trash and you're like, okay, is there?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, I can just throw this down too.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It's part of the issue.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Our streets aren't clean to the point where you think twice before you're adding your litter.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, I fully share your children's frustration and your frustration.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You know, I think one of the things that we are...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Endeavoring to achieve is a sense of pride and ownership in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think that is the most effective way we can solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Because again, I think everyone understands you are not supposed to throw things on the ground all across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And yet we see people do it.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And it is only when

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, when people think that they might get called out by their neighbors or they might get called out by their kids or they see that the street's clean and if I drop this one thing on the street, it then goes from clean to dirty, that they change their perspective.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so we are thinking through, you know, what are the many different mechanisms that we can use to achieve that sense of ownership and pride in our communities and look forward to working with you on how we can do that in your district specifically.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I will just add there that there are still fines for littering.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The city council did reduce those fines pretty substantially, not this council, but in, I think, around 2019.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we would be happy to have a conversation around increasing those.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Would love to have those conversations too.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I also think we need to piggyback off of your point.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I think one of the things that I have seen in the community is it's not the older folks that are littering.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's the new younger kids.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's the middle schoolers, the high schoolers, because they didn't have our campaigns that we had when we were growing up.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like we remember all the ads for don't litter, don't trash, and like all the like what it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They didn't grow up with any of that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So to us, that is the common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It is the common sense.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But I don't necessarily know if it is to all the generations after us.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So maybe an opportunity for a new marketing campaign.

chapters.summary: Vernikov asks what policies could encourage developers and contractors to reuse materials rather than dispose of them. Anderson references the draft SWAMP and work with EDC on deconstruction incentives. Jennifer McDonald details preliminary recoverable materials and an upcoming workshop with capital construction agencies.
chapters.title: Councilmember Vernikov questions Anderson on construction material reuse policies

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But alas, I will now turn it over to Councilmember Vernikov.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Really great points, both my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: And I would just add, Commissioner, to the couple of solutions you mentioned, just greater enforcement and fines.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: We have this issue in the district all the time.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: But other than that, I really want to thank the Department of Sanitation for being so great and wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: A couple questions I have.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Number one, just two questions.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: What policies could encourage developers and contractors to reuse materials rather than dispose of them?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's a great question and something that in our draft solid waste management plan, which we hope to finalize very shortly, we've started to dig into.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we're doing a lot of work right now with the Economic Development Corporation around those kinds of deconstruction rather than demolition incentives.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I'll let Jen speak to the details there.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: As the Commissioner mentioned, this swamp is the first time we're really shining a light on this material stream.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: In addition, the Council has included in their upcoming waste characterization law the requirement for characterizing the waste stream for this sector.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: And we think that will be really informative as far as developing programs and policies, as you mentioned, to target specific material types that have the highest value in recovery as part of the theme of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: Preliminarily, we're seeing things including asphalt, concrete.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: Perhaps even glass from construction and demolition as materials that can be sort of most easily circulated

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: and reused within our infrastructure here in the city because the technology exists, the companies exist that do this work and find ways to close those loops.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: We are continuing to engage both with EDC, as the commissioner mentioned, as well as the mayor's office of management and budget.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: We have put together a workshop this fall where all the capital construction agencies will be convening to take a closer look at many of these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: And we hope that that workshop will, as part of our SWAMP implementation, inform specific programs and policies that we should adopt to increase the recovery of these materials.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Vernikov raises health concerns about plastics, citing her father's plastics factory background, and asks about particular plastic packaging types of concern. Anderson discusses PFAS and forever chemicals but defers health questions to the Health Department, noting DSNY's expertise is in collection and remanufacturing.
chapters.title: Vernikov questions Anderson on plastic packaging health concerns

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: And the other question I have is about plastics.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Actually, my father back in the Ukraine owned a plastics factory that manufactured a lot of plastics products.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: So I actually know how dangerous it is to eat from plastics.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: And God forbid, some people microwave plastic.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: I've seen it myself.

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: So are there particular types of plastic packaging that present greater concerns in the New York City food system, if you could address that a little bit, whether it's packaging, bottled beverages, food preparation equipment, storage containers, or something else?

utterances.speaker: Inna Vernikov
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's a fantastic question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And certainly we've heard a lot of conversation in the last few years around PFAS and

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: other forever chemicals like that that are additives to plastic and other products that certainly have health impacts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: As far as the health implications of just different types of plastics, that's something that I think we'd have to defer to our colleagues at the health department on.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Our expertise is really on what happens to the

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: those products once we collect them and are we able to remanufacture them into new things.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But certainly there have been, I think, growing concerns expressed around the health implications of the amount of plastics that New Yorkers use.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Louis asks whether DSNY plans to promote bulk pickup services, noting most homeowners in her district are unaware. Anderson agrees it's a great idea and offers to work with her office on an education campaign, noting some bulk education was done during the composting rollout.
chapters.title: Councilmember Louis questions DSNY on bulk pickup promotion

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then I'm just going to turn it over to Councilmember Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And thank you, Commissioner, to you and your team for being here.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Just building on some of the questions that Councilmember Thomas Henry had, there's just one quick question.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I wanted to know, is DSNY planning to promote and share information about bulk pickup?

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I think most homeowners, particularly in my district, they don't know about bulk pickup unless they get, like, an email from my office or they come to a community board meeting.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And, you know, that's limited on the amount of people that come to those meetings.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I wonder if the agency is thinking about, like, a mass promotion and marketing about bulk pickups.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Maybe that could diminish some of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a great idea.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We did quite a bit of education around bulk collection as part of the rollout of our composting program because the set out days for some New Yorkers did change as we rolled out that program

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: because we're using a dual bin truck to collect the compostable material and trash side by side.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we ask that folks set out their bulk material on the non-recyclable.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Of the week, but we certainly can work with your office on an education campaign around bulk collection.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: That's a great idea.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: That would be super helpful.

chapters.summary: Louis asks about pilot composting sites removed from Flatbush Junction and East Flatbush in January, requesting help restoring or expanding composting. Anderson offers to work with her and reiterates universal curbside composting is available citywide.
chapters.title: Louis questions Anderson on removed composting sites in her district

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: My last question, we had a pilot composting site in my district that the district really enjoyed, but as of January of this year, those sites were removed.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: We had it for about two years and really enjoyed having those sites at the Flatbush Junction.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: We had another one that was in East Flatbush.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And those sites were removed.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And I wanted to know if there was any way I could work with the agency to either get those sites back or if there was any other programs that the agency provides to see if we could actually expand composting in our district.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: As we're having this conversation about safe disposals and waste management, it would be great to see if we could get like an actual program in the district.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we'd be happy to work with you on those composting sites.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I will just reiterate, we have a...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Universal curbside composting program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we pick up compostable material from every single residential building in New York City at least once a week.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think that's the first option that we'd encourage people to use, but we'll reach out and have a conversation around how we can increase participation in your district.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilman Lewis.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about other islands or city-owned land for composting. Anderson says most other islands have environmental protections or federal ownership restrictions, and DSNY is also exploring regional options outside NYC with private industry.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on additional city-owned land for composting beyond Rikers

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Speaking of composting, given that you mentioned Rikers and the opportunity for composting there, I wanted to know, are there any other islands

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: or city-owned land that you or the department are looking at for potential spots for composting as well?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're certainly always looking for potential locations for new compost facilities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think the challenge with a lot of the rest of New York City is that we are competing against other potential uses for city-owned property or even for privately owned property.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And in many cases, there are better uses.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Housing, for example, is a better use for much of the city's land than compost facilities.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think that's why we've really zeroed in on Rikers Island, because it's not really appropriate for residential development.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's a very large place.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's physically separated from other neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so it's sort of ripe for that kind of industrial use.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're also always...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Looking at this as a regional issue, because there is a substantial amount of property outside of New York City that may be a better use for or location for a compost facility.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we're always in conversations with the private industry around potential development of new sites that could take New York City material.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there any...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: like discussion about like some of the smaller islands and just turning into a compost island, like a brother, a brother island or, you know, any of those smaller places that, you know, are not.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Many of the other islands are either protected as either, you know, environmental,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: like conservation habitats or their property of the federal government or there are other kinds of restrictions on their use.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so there's complications with everything.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But if you have ideas, we're certainly happy to look at them.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about wet textile recyclability and curbside collection concerns given containerization. Anderson clarifies DSNY hasn't called textiles unrecyclable but notes two failed curbside pilots—rain damage and low demand—and suggests the next waste characterization study as the appropriate venue for further exploration.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on Intro 256 and curbside textile collection challenges

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to talk about Intro 256.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: This is Councilmember Hudson's bill in relation to requiring the commissioner to study the feasibility and potential environmental effects of recycling mandate for household textiles.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So in prior testimony, the department highlighted that wet textiles are unrecyclable.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the agency provide additional information on why that is the case for textiles, but not other waste streams like paper?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And with the requirement of citywide containerization, is this still a concern?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't know that we've testified that they're unrecyclable.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think the department's position in the past has been that curbside collection of textiles presents some really unique challenges that may be difficult to overcome.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we have actually in two different occasions piloted curbside collection of textiles and sort of proven out what these challenges look like.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The first was a pilot that we did maybe a decade ago in parts of Brooklyn where we did a curbside collection.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We actually sent these pink bags out to residents and said, you know, put all your textiles in these pink bags.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We're coming on this day and we'll pick them up.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We found a couple things there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: One, if it rains, it really destroys the quality of the textiles and the ability to reuse those textiles.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So then you're automatically downcycling them into lesser products.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Number two, just the sort of...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Operational barriers to operating a program like that, I think would make it very expensive to scale.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We also had an appointment-based program in, I think, around 2022, 23, where we, this was on Staten Island, where Staten Islanders could make appointments for the collection of textiles.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We saw really, really low demand for that program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think, you know, both of those sort of indicate that curbside collection may not be the way to go.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But we are, you know, open to exploring other collection models.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, I think if this bill were to pass, I think the appropriate sort of space to do that would be as part of our next waste characterization study, which is due in January of 28.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the 2,500 enrolled buildings, average bin counts per building, and bin locations. Anderson explains larger buildings may have multiple bins, most need one, bins are in basements or trash rooms, and pickups occur on demand when bins are full.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on textile recycling program enrollment and bin details

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: You said earlier, if I'm wrong, 31,000 residential buildings were registered in enrolled in the textile recycling program.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's 2,500 buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But those 2,500 buildings represent a substantial number of actual units of residential housing.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so what is the average number of textile collection bins distributed to residential properties enrolled in the program?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Just one?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It depends on the size of the building.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: For a larger building, that 2,500 number could include large residential complexes.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Those may have multiple bins, but for most buildings, we find that one bin is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And because we pick it up whenever it's full, if it fills up once a week, we'll pick it up once a week.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If it fills up once every six months, we'll pick it up every six months.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And do you generally know where the textile collection bins in these buildings are generally located?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Where are they generally located?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, often they're in, it was a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Often they're located in the basements or in the trash storage room or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I've also seen them in some buildings in the parking garage if they have one.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So it really varies based on the space they have.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about outreach to property owners and requests a breakdown of textile waste collected by participant category. Anderson describes standard apartment building outreach covering multiple programs and says DSNY will provide the data.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions DSNY on textile outreach and participant category breakdown

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And what kind of outreach is done to a property owner about the existence of this program?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, the outreach is part of our standard apartment building outreach.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So anytime we're having conversations with multi-unit buildings, we talk to them about the textile collection program, the electronics collection program, the requirements for recycling, the requirements to have a brown bin.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's all sort of part of one package of outreach that we do.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Of the eligible program participant categories, so the apartment buildings with 10 plus units, office buildings, commercial industries, and schools and nonprofit institutions, can the department provide a breakdown of the amount of textile waste collected by each participant category?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We don't have that with us today, but we can certainly dig into the data and provide you whatever we can.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Awesome.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the timeline for a small residential building textile pilot and the collection partner. Kate Kitchener says they hope to pilot within a year and the partner is Helpsy, a B Corp.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions DSNY on small residential textile pilot timeline and collection partner

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And can the department provide a timeline for the launch of the small residential buildings textile recycling pilot program?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, we're working with our vendor right now to look at all the details of how that's going to work.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And we're hoping to pilot something in the next year.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Awesome.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks why textile bins seem emptier after switching from Housing Works to DSNY's program. Kitchener explains Housing Works was a nonprofit offering tax write-offs while Helpsy is a B Corp that cannot, but Helpsy collects more frequently. Anderson adds Housing Works struggled with logistics at scale.
chapters.title: Sanchez and Kitchener discuss Helpsy vs Housing Works textile program transition

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So you mentioned a partner originally with the residential textile program.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Who is that partner?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, we partner with a B Corp called Helpsee.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: They're doing the textile collection.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: One of the things is with the residential buildings, one of the things I'm curious about is, so I used to have in my building, for example, it used to be like a Housing Works textile recycling program that had
