utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: tabs that you could take off, and it was a tax write-off that you donated your textiles.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I remember that textile thing being...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Packed all the time.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And now anytime that I pass by the textile thing, it's usually rather empty, but there's a brand new sign that says that now it's the Department of Sanitation one and there is no tax write-off.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm curious to know, is there a difference in the buildings that

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: you know, in the areas where buildings have that are participating in these programs.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like, did you have buildings before that had a lot of textile recycling and now don't because they're not getting their tax?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like, for example, is the Upper West Side not going to be...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they get their tax write-off?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: I think a couple of things there.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So, yeah, our prior...

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Our contract was with Housing Works, which is a nonprofit.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Our new contract is with Help C.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: It's a B Corp, so they are not technically a nonprofit, so you can't do the tax write-offs.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: They do work with Goodwill and a lot of other partners.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: A lot of the clothing does end up going to nonprofits, but because they have the B Corp status, they can't actually do the tax donation receipt, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: I think the other thing that's happening is that our new partner has been doing much more frequent collections, so you might be seeing the bin empty because it's getting emptied more frequently instead of overflowing.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So we actually think that's a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'll just add there that when we had the previous contract with Housing Works, they really struggled to match the scale of the program, which, as we've discussed, is not as big as we'd like it to be.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And there were points toward the end of our agreement with Housing Works where they were subcontracting the collections to HelpSee anyway.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So when we put the contract out for rebid, I think it made sense to go with a provider that could accommodate the scale of the program and that really excelled in the sort of operational capacity.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Housing Works is a fantastic organization.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: They do a lot of really good work.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But logistics at that scale, I think, was a challenge for them.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: But yeah, that was just a thing.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If the tax abatement does anything for folks.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY tracks abandoned delivery courier bags and can hold companies responsible. Anderson says DSNY doesn't formally track them, is exploring existing enforcement tools, and is open to working with the Council on new tools if needed.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on tracking abandoned last-mile delivery courier bags

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then finally,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the department track the volume of delivery?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: courier bags, such as those used by last mile delivery services that it collects and disposes of?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then under the existing commercial waste rules, does the department have the authority to hold last mile delivery companies responsible for abandoned reusable textile equipment?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I will say on a formal basis, no, we do not track the number of those last mile delivery courier bags that we see.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I personally take a photograph every time I see one.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so I have my own little side project there.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think, you know, anyone who spends time walking around New York City has probably seen them discarded all across the city.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So it's something that we are looking into whether we have existing enforcement tools to be able to hold those companies accountable.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And if our existing tools aren't sufficient, we're certainly interested in working with the council to develop new tools that we can use.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Hunts Point is a great artist community.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We have an Amazon Last Mile delivery facility there.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if you ever want to throw a little art show with all of your photos, we are happy to help.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I would like to now recognize Councilmember Virginia Maloney and Ty Hankerson in some updated swag.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I would like to turn it over to Councilmember Santa Suoso.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks why buildings reject textile bins and about incentives for participation. Kitchener cites stairs and space as barriers and mentions exploring smaller containers. Santosuosso notes no Helpsy drop-off sites in Bay Ridge and asks about incentives like sanitation credits. Anderson suggests continuing nonprofit donations for tax write-offs and offers to brainstorm creative incentives.
chapters.title: Councilmember Santosuosso questions DSNY on textile recycling participation barriers

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Always repping Hunt's point.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Mostly on textiles.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: When you do your outreach to the residential buildings about potentially taking on a bin, what are some of the reasons that the buildings reject it?

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, so I mean, I think the selling point to having the bin is that, you know, the laundry rooms and basements of a lot of these buildings are like kind of full of textiles anyway, and it's a mess.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And having the bin, you know, makes it cleaner, it's tidier.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And so a lot of the building supers really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Some of the challenges are like potentially having stairs can be a problem sometimes if there's not an elevator to get the bin down there.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And then space is the other thing.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: And we've actually done some research and totally open to ideas around another container besides the bin, something smaller.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: So that's definitely something that we're looking at and continuing to explore.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: When I first heard, I think it was on a Zoom call that I first heard about the textile recycling program.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I didn't know it existed.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I have since, well, I know there are some buildings in Bay Ridge that have them in the residential buildings, but we actually have no, I looked on the map recently, we have no drop-off sites through the HelpSee partner.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So I'm just thinking of ways to try to encourage people to participate in the residential program or have some of these bins in the more public sites.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Are there incentives that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I understand HelpSee is not a nonprofit, so there's no sort of tax write-off.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Are there, is there a possibility of like a sanitation credit that could be applied against future fines and fees?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Or is there some other incentive that you can think of that could encourage participation?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's a very interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: You can, if you donate your textiles through Goodwill, Housing Works, Salvation Army, many other thrift stores that are nonprofits, you can still claim that tax write-off.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I'd encourage you, I'd encourage all New Yorkers that if that's a priority for them, that they should continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But certainly, you know, we can work with you on thinking about new creative incentives for how to encourage that kind of behavior.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Do you know how many city-owned buildings have the textile recycling bins?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It's in the report that there are some in schools.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't have those numbers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Kate Kitchener
utterances.text: There are a few in schools, and we, of course, have them in our sanitation offices.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks about gaps and approaches to corner dumping on litter baskets. Anderson identifies challenges in mixed commercial-residential streets without space for official bins, proposes shared Empire bins with access cards, and notes DSNY already has enforcement tools but needs resources.
chapters.title: Santosuosso questions Anderson on corner dumping and shared container solutions

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And then my only other question was about going back to the dumping piece that Councilmember Thomas Henry was speaking about.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Our district deals with a lot of just corner dumping on baskets, which blows my mind because, as you said, Commissioner, it's like we will pick up the trash.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: The service is available to you.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Have you identified gaps and or, you know, approaches to some of the corner dumping that we could help move legislation along or try to address in any way?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, I think, yes, there are certainly gaps.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think in your district in particular and many other districts in sort of southern Brooklyn, I think one of the biggest challenges that we see is in places where

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: you have first floor commercial and one or two stories of residential above.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: There may not be a good place.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: for the official New York City bin, which is now required as of this week.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, people just have been used to taking their trash to the corner litter basket, which is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think when we roll out the Empire bins, I think one of the places that we really want to look at the opportunity for shared containers is on streets exactly like that,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: where potentially we could put one Empire bin for the entire street, give access cards to every resident on that street, and have them use that instead of other kinds of containers for their waste set out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And that would really streamline things and give them a designated place that they can put their trash without having to manage a bin without any space to do so.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So that's certainly something that we're thinking about as far as enforcement tools.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We at this point have a lot of tools at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If we see any identifying information either in a litter basket or adjacent to a litter basket, we can write a ticket based on that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We do so pretty frequently.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I don't think it's a matter of having more tools.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think it's just the resources to be out there and do the enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether an EIS will be done for Rikers composting and flags traffic concerns through residential neighborhoods and LaGuardia Airport operations. Anderson says environmental review will be part of the process and DSNY would explore waterway transport to minimize impacts.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry questions Anderson on Rikers Island composting EIS and traffic concerns

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And I will turn it over to Councilmember Shanel-Thomas-Henry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to go right back to the composting or just all organic waste processing anticipated for Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Was there an EIS done for that, or will there be?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And that is all from Kaltz.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So at this point, we don't have a formal capital project or really any specific plans for doing so.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: It's something that we are exploring.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I know that the city, particularly under this administration, has been moving more and more

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: decommissioned jail properties from DOC to DCAS to begin the process of planning for the post-jail future of Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And there would certainly be an environmental review done as part of that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, I just want to flag because although the island itself is isolated, there is currently only one roadway in, and it goes through a residential neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And in addition to the residents, there is a baseball field at that corner.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if you're aware, but the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey with LaGuardia Airport uses what they call Ingram's Mountain adjacent to that for higher vehicle parking currently.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So just to be cognizant of, and I would recommend kind of collaborating with them on any movement.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: out of there from a traffic perspective and then looking at any other ways of getting the waste over there like the waterways or what have you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And, you know, one of the things that I think the Department of Sanitation has been a longtime leader in is using our city's waterways to move material around.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Most of our recyclables and much of our trash moves on the water today.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And I think we would certainly look for opportunities to move compostable material by water as well to any potential future Rikers compost facility.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry notes a recurring theme that residents are unaware of DSNY programs and urges creative marketing campaigns, praising DSNY staff member Frank. Anderson responds that DSNY lacks a public education or advertising budget and would like to work with the Council on budget requests for marketing.
chapters.title: Thomas-Henry urges DSNY to improve public awareness of programs and marketing

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, and I did just want to end on a comment.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It seems to be a recurring theme that sanitation does a lot of great programs, but it has a lot of great programs that many people...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And with that, I yell my time.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And with that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Has a lot of great, that people just aren't aware of.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So just really thinking about your marketing campaign.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I mean, and the admin, the mayor is great on social media.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I mean, I hear about potholes from here to L.A.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So just.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thinking of getting creative on how letting the public know about a lot of the programs, encouraging them not to litter, and all the things.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And I want to shout out Frank.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: He is amazing, and you guys do a great job.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And we are always looking for free ways to get out the word.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We unfortunately don't have a public education budget.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So every conversation that we have with buildings,

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: has to happen through sort of organic and natural means.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We do a lot of work on social media to try to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We do a lot of work through the traditional media to try to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But unlike other agencies, we don't have an advertising budget.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We don't have a marketing budget that we can lean on.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so that's something that we would love to work with the council on as part of the budget next year.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I love the idea of agencies with advertising budgets.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like we have some bills about that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: We will circle back.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about Intro 970, requesting headcounts for the targeted neighborhood task force and precision cleaning initiative, and whether they overlap. Anderson says the programs now operate as fungible resources without specific schedules, deployed based on identified cleaning needs.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on nightlife district cleaning programs and staffing

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to talk briefly about Councilmember Gutierrez's bill.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So you can finish these questions.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the, for those, again, it is in relation to the enhanced street cleaning and litter basket services in a proposed nightlife districts.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the department provide a headcount for the targeted neighborhood task force and the precision cleaning initiative?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are these teams exclusive or is there an overlap between the task force and initiative?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And for the task force, how are staff assigned to neighborhoods and likewise for the initiative?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't have those numbers directly in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Hold on, I'll try to pull them up.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, we don't have those numbers directly in front of us.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But I will say, you know, the targeted neighborhood task force and precision cleaning initiative, even though those were sort of funded as separate programs, they now operate as much more fungible assets.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So there isn't necessarily a specific frequency or schedule with which we're using them.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We identify conditions that need to be cleaned, and then we sort of draw from that pool of resources as we are cleaning those conditions.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about late-night and early-morning street cleaning frequency. Anderson says overnight litter basket service is effective, but Sunday coverage is lower because it requires double-time overtime outside the regular Monday-Saturday work week.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on overnight street cleaning and Sunday staffing

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the department conduct any late night or early morning street cleaning or litter basket servicing?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the frequency of these services and at what dates and times of the week?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I know some of this because my street cleaning is from 12 to 3 a.m.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yes, we do quite a lot of overnight litter basket service because, one, it's the best time for us to sort of move around the city and get the work done quickly.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Two, because we can sort of, you know, come through after the last of the, you know, the...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Bar goers go home for the evening and clean things up before people start to go to work or school in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So we find that a really effective time to do so.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I would say probably the one time that is the most challenge for us is late Saturday night into Sunday morning, just because Monday through Saturday are regular work days for us.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Sunday is not a regular work day.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So any work that we do on Sundays is double time overtime and has to be sort of pulled out of a separate pot of resources.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so we do have a slightly lower number of resources on that 12 to 8 shift Sunday than we would on the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm curious about that.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there, so just a standard work week for every sanitation employee, even though we have to clean the streets seven days a week, is Monday through Friday?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Monday through Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Monday through Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Interesting.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about staggering worker schedules to cover Sundays. Anderson explains workers already stagger across six days but making Sunday a regular workday would require labor negotiations with the Teamsters in the next round.
chapters.title: Sanchez and Anderson discuss staggering sanitation worker schedules for Sunday coverage

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Has there been no discussion on just staggering workers'work weeks?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Like some people work Tuesday through Sunday.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Some people work Monday through Friday.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's the practice for covering the six-day, because each individual works five days over the course of a six-day period.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So, you know, we do stagger the shifts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think a conversation about having Sunday be a scheduled workday would have to be something that we would bring up as part of labor negotiations with the Teamsters in the next round of negotiations, which we expect will begin in the next year or so.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether DSNY provides supplemental cleaning to high-traffic or nightlife districts. Anderson confirms DSNY tailors service levels based on density, transit, and land use, noting existing nightlife resources on the Lower East Side and opportunities in growing outer-borough nightlife districts like Hunts Point and Bushwick.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on supplemental cleaning for high-density and nightlife areas

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the department already provide other supplemental cleaning services to community districts with higher density of pedestrian foot traffic or nightlife establishments?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And can you describe the extent of those services and the resources dedicated to such programs?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, we absolutely tailor our service levels.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: based on a number of factors, and that can include the density of bus and subway routes in an area, the amount of commuting traffic, the amount of pedestrian traffic, other kinds of

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: land uses in a district.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so I think that's what drives a lot of our resource allocation today.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Nightlife is certainly a part of that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I remember this was maybe eight or nine years ago when the prior two administrations ago when they created the Office of Nightlife as part of

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: cultural affairs, there was a real push to reallocate some resources to those nightlife districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And some of that is still in place today, particularly on the Lower East Side.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But I think there, you know, as this bill indicates, there's more opportunity, particularly in parts of the outer boroughs that are now growing nightlife districts.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Hunts Point is one.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think East Williamsburg and Bushwick is another where there's certainly room for more resources if we had the funding.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Brooklyn has taken the throne.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I mean, it's the reality.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I mean, Manhattan nightlife, step it up.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How has the, and that's no shade.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's no shade.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It's just, we have to be real about what's happening.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how commercial waste zones implementation has affected litter basket waste in high-foot-traffic areas. Anderson says there's no measurable impact on litter basket collections, as improper disposal is largely by residents rather than commercial establishments.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on commercial waste zones impact on litter basket waste

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How has the implementations of commercial waste soads impacted the amount of waste collected at public litter baskets and during street cleaning in areas with high foot traffic and pedestrian traffic?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Foot traffic.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that we've seen a real measurable impact on litter basket collections as a result of the rollout of commercial waste zones.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: If anything, I think we have better data on the commercial establishments and limiting the improper disposal that commercial establishments are doing.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But I think for a long time that improper disposal has been happening by residents, and so it doesn't really have an impact there.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how many parcels DOC has transferred for Rikers composting. Anderson says two large contiguous parcels have been transferred to DCAS plus decommissioned jail facilities, though buildings need demolition first. Sanchez asks about repurposing jail buildings; Anderson says composting requires large open spaces.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on Rikers Island parcel transfers for composting

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And before we go back to co-digestion and Hunt's point once again, I just want to circle back quickly to the composting on Rikers Island question.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: It has, or do we know how many parcels the Department of Corrections has transferred or will transfer once?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Rikers is a figment of our imaginations.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so there are two quite sizable parcels that have been transferred to DCAS as well as a number of jail facilities that have been decommissioned and transferred.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I think that the challenge with the jail facilities, as we've had conversations with DCAS and others, is you have to demolish the buildings that are there, and that's sort of the first step.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I know that the city, through DCAS, is looking at opportunities to begin that demolition process.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: But we are...

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Predominantly looking at the two large contiguous.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: parcels that have been transferred.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there no, probably a side note, do Haxa actually demolish all of the jails?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there no way to activate, you know, maybe gut the inside of and turn it into something fresh and new?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't think you could use any of the existing buildings for composting purposes because you need sort of large open spaces for composting and jails are not known for those.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Large open spaces.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks for average daily collection of source-separated residential organics and landfill diversion estimates. Anderson reports 80,000 tons of organics collected year-to-date and promises to provide the daily average.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Anderson on residential organics collection tonnage and diversion

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay, turning our attention to co-digestion.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the average daily collection in pounds of source-separated residential organic waste?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the department provide an estimate of the amount of organic waste diverted from landfills due to curbside collection of residential organic waste?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So year to date this year, we've collected 80,000 tons of organics.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: I don't have the average daily in front of me here.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Trying to do the math quickly.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: We'll get back to you with the average daily, but it's 80,000 tons so far this year.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about current capacity to process residential and commercial organic waste by anaerobic digestion and future improvements. Jennifer McDonald describes eight processing locations including two anaerobic digestion facilities—Newtown Creek in Brooklyn and one in New Jersey. Jane Gajwani reports Newtown Creek processes about 250 tons per day.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions DSNY and DEP on anaerobic digestion capacity and processing facilities

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can the department provide an estimate for, not the daily, what is the city's current capacity to process residential and commercial organic waste by anaerobic digestion?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And how might this capacity improve in the next 10 years?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'll let Jen start and then maybe we'll pass it over to Jane at DP.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: The department has a number of transfer stations and processing facilities that we send the collected curbside organics to.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: There's actually eight distinct locations.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: Many of them are transfer stations, so from there they move the material to either a composting facility or an anaerobic digestion facility, maybe in city, maybe out of city, as the commissioner mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: We are part of a regional network of managing resources, including organics.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: So some of the capacity that ultimately processes the material that we collect is outside of the city.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: Of the two anaerobic digestion facilities that are being used today for the material that's collected, one is in New Jersey and the other is the Department of Environmental Protection's Newtown Creek facility in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer McDonald
utterances.text: And Jane from DEP is here to speak to us and can share how much material that facility is processing on an average basis.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So at the Newtown Creek facility, we can currently process about 250 tons a day of material, so 500,000 pounds a day.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And that's from both Department of Sanitation, but also from the commercial sector.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And it's typically two-thirds from sanitation, about a third from the commercial sector, but that can vary seasonally or other schools are in session, things like that.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how much renewable natural gas Newtown Creek produces annually and how it's used. Gajwani says it's enough to heat about 6,500 homes, with the gas distributed into National Grid's system as renewable natural gas, monetized through the federal renewable fuel standard.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on renewable natural gas production at Newtown Creek

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And speaking of Newtown Creek, how much renewable natural gas is produced annually by the facility?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I don't have that number offhand, but I do know that it is enough to heat the homes of about 6,500 homes in the city.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And so the city just uses that renewable heat to heat homes, and is it just sold within the city?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So the actual molecules of methane, of natural gas, that leave Newtown Creek are distributed into National Grid's natural gas distribution system as renewable natural gas, as a non-fossil alternative to natural gas.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: There are different programs to monetize the environmental attributes of the renewable natural gas.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so currently National Grid is participating in the federal renewable fuel standard.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so that allows them to kind of.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Be able to

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: get revenue for being able to provide a renewable resource within the fossil infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And we work with them to try and kind of maximize that so that they're able to pay off the large capital investment that they had made in their system sooner.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about DEP's 2023 RFEI soliciting customers for biodigester methane. Gajwani reports strong interest and identifies the key opportunity of new digesters at Hunts Point, where excess biogas could be converted to renewable natural gas replicating the Newtown Creek model.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on RFEI for biodigester methane and Hunts Point plans

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: DEP published a RFEI soliciting potential customers for biodigester methane.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you provide any updates pertaining to that solicitation?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So, yes, we put it out, and as you might be aware, we have 14 in-city wastewater treatment plants, and all of them have anaerobic digesters.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we have 75 anaerobic digesters spread across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: As a result of that solicitation, we did get a lot of really interesting feedback, a lot of key opportunities from kind of, you know, things that could happen within, you know, the next five to ten years to things that could happen, you know, 50 years out.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And one of the key opportunities that was identified and, you know, we had kind of already been working on anticipating that it was going to come is that we're building these new digesters at the Hunts Point facility in the South Bronx, which you're familiar with.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And that's, you know, there's excess biogas that's going to be generated there.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: There's an opportunity there to take the excess biogas.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we use the gas, right, to heat our buildings seasonally and also to heat the digesters year-round.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But there is excess biogas, and so that biogas can be beneficially.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: used and so we actually would like to replicate the model of Newtown Creek to be able to take that excess biogas and convert it to a renewable natural gas as a non-fossil alternative.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about anaerobic digester operating costs and the Newtown Creek co-digestion pilot cost breakdown. Gajwani says the pilot operates at no cost to the city, with costs borne by Waste Management, and that she doesn't have specific operating cost numbers.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on anaerobic digester operating costs and co-digestion pilot

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And how much does it cost to operate the anaerobic digester?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: The anaerobic digesters themselves.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So that's, I don't have those numbers offhand.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I can see if we can actually tease out those numbers from the operation of our different facilities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Can DEP provide a cost breakdown for the Newtown Creek co-digestion pilot?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So the pilot has been done as a, it's a program that's kind of at no cost to the city.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So all of those costs are borne by our partner, Waste Management.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we actually don't have those specific numbers.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how co-digestion impacts operating costs and about cost-sharing arrangements. Gajwani explains biogas processing is at no cost to the city through agreements with Waste Management and National Grid, but there are costs for heating food waste, biosolids disposal, and nitrogen management, offset by Waste Management payments.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on co-digestion cost impacts and shared costs with partners

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: How does co-digestion of organic waste impact operation costs?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the biogas processing facility contribute to cost?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And you've already spoken about how you've shared costs with waste management and National Grid.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Is there any other ways that you share costs with them as well?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So the actual processing of the biogas is similar to the contract that we have with waste management, where it's at no cost to the city.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We have an agreement with National Grid where it's also at no cost to the city.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: However, within the processing itself, there are energy.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: costs for kind of heating up the food waste.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: It only makes up about 10% of the total mass that we're putting into the digesters, but there is, you know, heat associated with that.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then in the actual processing, you know, the biogas itself is, you know, kind of not at additional cost to us, but the

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: the residual, the amount of the food waste that does not convert to biogas, it's about 25% of the incoming mass

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: that becomes biosolids, and then that has a disposal cost and recycling cost associated with it, as does, you know, there's different constituents of the food waste, such as nitrogen.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We have sensitive waterways from a nitrogen standpoint, and so we have to make sure that we're managing the nitrogen appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So there's costs associated with that.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We have a cost offset that we receive from waste management that covers the costs of the additional costs to DEP just in the processing of the additional food waste.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the status of Hunts Point wastewater facility upgrades and when digesters will be operational. Gajwani says construction should end this year, digesters operational by next calendar year, with follow-on contracts for energy efficiency and odor control.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on Hunts Point facility construction status and timeline

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Now, moving on to Hunts Point, the new wastewater resource recovery facility.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So not new, but updated, new and improved.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In August of 2025, a DAP newsletter stated that infrastructure upgrades to the Hunts Point facility were approximately 75% complete.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the current status of the site improvement work, and when are the anaerobic digesters expected to be operational?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I believe that the...

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Construction is supposed to end this year, so by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And, yeah, those digesters should be up and running by the next calendar year.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then there are follow-on contracts to that particular contract.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we're in design and going to be putting out to bid a new contract for energy efficiency improvements and also odor control.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether the 250 ton/day capacity includes biosolids and how much remains for curbside organics. Gajwani says Hunts Point could potentially handle up to 400 tons/day of food waste but nitrogen management studies are ongoing, so the final number will be lower.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on Hunts Point processing capacity for organic waste

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Does the 250 ton per day processing capacity for organic waste include biosolids recovered on site?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If so, approximately how many or how much capacity remains for organic waste from the curbside and smart bin streams?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: At Hans Point specifically.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we're still studying that.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We know that within the digester capacity itself, we could do potentially up to 400 tons a day of food waste processing, co-digestion.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: However, we need to kind of, that's just kind of one piece of the puzzle.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We need to look at kind of, you know, I had mentioned earlier about we have to make sure that we're managing the nitrogen properly.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we're doing an assessment of how much additional nitrogen we can handle within our system without impacting our waterways.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so that's something, it's a study that's ongoing right now and that we're trying to get a final number on.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But it will be south of 400 tons a day, most likely.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how organics will be transported to Hunts Point and about storage and odor impacts on nearby residents. Gajwani describes the pre-processing and enclosed vessel process, interest in partnering with the adjacent food market, and exploring waterway transport to minimize community impacts.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on organics transport and community impact at Hunts Point

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And how will the organics processed at the facility be transported to the site for processing?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Will the waste need to be...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Stored on site prior to co-digestion?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And if so, what steps will DSNY or DEP take to limit the impact on the residents that live next to the facility?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So there's a few pieces to this, and Jen might want to weigh in on this as well.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But so the food waste that's collected curbside or that are coming from private haulers, there's a really important step that needs to take place where there's pre-processing.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so for the Newtown Creek facility that we have, waste management has a waste transfer station where they do this pre-processing, where they take out all of the physical contamination, and then they kind of macerate it and thin it down so that it's pumpable.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so then they can put these into vector trucks that can then go, you know, kind of the mile from their facility to our facility.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then it gets put into a tank.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: These are all kind of enclosed vessels, so there's not a tremendous amount of odor concerns with them.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then it goes into our storage tank that happens in batches, obviously, because they're truck deliveries.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then, you know, from the storage tank, then it is evenly brought over to the digesters because the microbiome and the digester is like a steady diet of material, of organics.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So that's kind of how that process works for the Hunts Point facility.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We are interested in looking at alternatives for transportation.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: It would be great if we could partner with the food market next to it.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And so then that would be kind of a very easy transfer.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So that's one example of kind of keeping it very local.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We're also interested in and have been talking to EDC if there's ways to move this material, as Commissioner Anderson had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: New York City has this long history of moving material by waterways, and so we'd like to see that as well.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We really want to keep any impacts to the local community at a minimum.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: That was my very next question is I'm really excited to hear about the partnership, especially with the markets next door.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about barge transport volumes, potential truck traffic, air pollution impacts, and mitigation for high asthma rates in his district. Gajwani estimates possibly 15 trucks/day at full capacity, discusses alternatives like electric or CNG trucks, and notes environmental assessments will be needed.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on barge vs truck transport and air pollution mitigation

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Will marine and barge transfer be utilized for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And, you know.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: If so, approximately how much waste are we looking that will be transported to the site via barge each day and how much potentially via truck if we have to use that?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Yeah, so we don't have those details yet, and it's something that we'll definitely, right, we need to figure out first how much material can we actually take in, you know, in theory, and then look at kind of what are the ways to bring it in, and there would need to be, you know, an environmental assessment of how that works as well.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So there's logistics to be considered and then also the environmental assessment.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: So, you know, if we are unlucky that we have to be transporting via truck,

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to be cognizant and understand approximately how many trucks per day will be transporting organics to be processed at this site.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, what are the projected...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: air pollutions and carbon emission ramifications associated with trucking waste to the facility.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And given already, I don't have to tell people the high asthma rates in my district, are any mitigation efforts being considered to address any increase in truck traffic to the site?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So knowing that we receive like eight to 10 trucks a day at the Newtown Creek facility, if we were to actually do the full 400 tons a day at Hunts Point, we might be talking about 15 or so trucks a day.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: That's kind of off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: It's not an official number.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: If we were to move all of it via truck, and I think that there are different alternatives to be considered for trucks, right, as far as like, you know, if it's a short haul, is there a way to electrify the trucks?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Or is there, you know, kind of, could they be CNG instead of, you know, diesel?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Could they use our RNG, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Like, are there kind of different ways to do this so that the emissions are kept at a minimum?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Yeah, really appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks whether Hunts Point will digest engineered bioslurry from Waste Management. Gajwani explains DEP is seeking an owner's advisor for contracting, the market has matured, and they want an integrated partner for both pre-processed food waste delivery and biogas cleanup.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on bioslurry digestion and Hunts Point contracting plans

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Will this site also be digesting engineered bioslurry produced by waste management?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we will put this out for a solicitation.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So we actually put out a request for proposals back in the spring for an owner's advisor to help us kind of navigate how we're going to contract the work at Hunts Point for both co-digestion and the...

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: the gas-to-grid system.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: We currently have, as I just, you know, as I mentioned before, we have two contracts at Newtown Creek, and they're good contracts, but they were kind of put together right when the, you know, this industry or this kind of market was very new.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: In the ensuing, you know, 14 years or so, the market has really matured, and so we are getting an owner's advisor to make sure that we're kind of making the right decisions for the city, for DEP,

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: and, you know, kind of leveraging kind of the lessons learned from municipalities across the world that have been doing this type of work.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So it's unclear whether it would be a partnership, ultimately be a partnership with waste management or another partner, but we are anticipating that we would like to have an integrated partner that does both, that brings us the pre-processed food waste, as

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: waste management calls it, engineered bioslurry, but it's something of that ilk that meets our specifications for treatment, and then would also be able to clean up the biogas for beneficial use.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks how much RNG will be produced daily at Hunts Point and what proportion used on-site. Gajwani estimates output similar to Newtown Creek (enough for 6,500 homes), with about 50-60% used on-site seasonally and the remainder distributed to the grid.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani on renewable natural gas output and on-site usage at Hunts Point

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And approximately how much renewable natural gas will be produced per day?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: What proportion of that methane will be used on site?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And how will the remainder be utilized?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I believe that, and again, this is...

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Anticipating the maximum amount of food waste that we talked about, which is about 400 tons a day.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Let me just do a really, I think that the, you know, I don't have that number in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I'm trying to like quickly calculate.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: I could just get back to you on the total number, but it's probably in the same range of what we have for Newtown Creek, which is...

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: 6,500 homes, enough gas to heat 6,500 homes.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: As far as how much is used on site, it varies seasonally.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But I think similar to Newtown Creek, I feel like it was on average about 50 or 60% would be used on site.

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about odor control solutions at Hunts Point and complaint handling. Gajwani describes enclosed digestion processes, odor control upgrades in follow-on contracts, and DEP's 311 response. Anderson adds that DEC regulates odors at transfer stations and DSNY conducts weekly inspections.
chapters.title: Sanchez questions Gajwani and Anderson on odor control at digestion facilities

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And then studies have shown that sulfurous and...

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Nitrogenous compounds are generated from anaerobic digestion operations, and they can be released into the air and

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: during dewatering and storage with all the unpleasant smells, leading to a deterioration in the quality of life in neighboring communities.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Are there any odor control solutions that have been designed into the digester at the Hunts Point facility?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And in general, has the Department of Sanitation or DEP noticed a frequency of odor complaints at any of the other currently operating digester facilities in the city?

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And what agency handles those complaints, DSNY or DEP?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The world wants to know.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So I do know that the current, so the contract, the follow-on contract to the digester contract at Hunts Point does have odor control associated with it, and that is specifically for the solids handling

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: portion of the...

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Of the wastewater treatment process, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So that's where the thickening process and the transferring, the storage process.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: So that's, you know, that particular odor control system is being upgraded as part of the next round of construction that we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: As far as the additional facilities, I am actually unfamiliar with the odor complaints that may have been received from associated with the solids handling and the digestion.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Digestion itself is a closed, you know, kind of containerized process.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But you're right, like, you know, kind of as you move material over to dewatering, there could be odors.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: All of our dewatering buildings have odor control associated with them.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But, you know, there could be excursions here or there.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And I know that people do send complaints to 311, and the DEP is very responsive to them.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: they immediately go out and they, you know, kind of monitor the area to kind of look for where the concerns may be.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: Sometimes it could be a door that's just left open as they're kind of moving bins in and out.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: And then they tend to rectify that quickly.

utterances.speaker: Jane Gajwani
utterances.text: But I'm not sure if there's additional details.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'll add that.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Both DEP facilities and public and private transfer stations are regulated by the State Department of Environmental Conservation, and they take odor complaints very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: So I think that's sort of the first avenue for those sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: The Department of Sanitation also regulates private transfer stations, and we conduct inspections on a very regular basis, at least weekly, of every transfer station in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: One of the things we're looking for is, you know, are the odors, the leachate, the other things that are sort of happening inside the transfer station, are they exiting the transfer station in any way?

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: And so, you know, that is enforcement that we do on a very regular basis.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks DSNY and DEP witnesses for their testimony, notes the importance of protecting the park near the Hunts Point facility, and announces a five-minute break before public testimony begins.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks agency witnesses and announces short break before public testimony

chapters.summary: Eric Goldstein of NRDC supports Intro 256 for textile recycling study, suggests analyzing non-DSNY collection options and tracking what happens to collected textiles, supports Intro 970 and both resolutions, and urges the Council to review and strengthen the draft Solid Waste Management Plan.
chapters.title: Eric Goldstein (NRDC) testifies in support of Intro 256 and SWAMP review

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Sanchez, and welcome to your new committee council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: My name is Eric Goldstein.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: I'm the New York City Environment Director at the Natural Resources Defense Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: NRDC strongly supports Intro 256, which would mandate that DSNY study the source separation of textiles in their collection by the Department of Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Textiles make up between 5 and 6 percent of the city's municipal solid waste.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Their manufacture and disposal is an environmental problem, a climate problem, and a budgetary burden for New York City residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: We make one important friendly suggestion to the proposed language of Intro 256.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: In addition to studying the possibility of textile collection by the department, we urge the council to direct ESNY to analyze other options for textile collection, including expansion of the current system in place for some multi-story buildings now run in cooperation, as you've heard,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: with HELPSI and the New York State Industries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: for the disabled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: And additionally, we recommend that the council ensure that the bill language directs DSNY to examine what happens to textiles that are collected for recycling and whether and how those materials are actually reused or recycled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: We also support Intro 970, which would enhance street cleaning and litter basket service in certain New York City neighborhoods, and the two resolutions before the Council today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: But the most pressing matter for this committee to engage in in the weeks ahead, we respectfully suggest, is to review and enhance the draft solid waste management plan prepared by DSNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: The current draft prepared by DSNY needs help, and in several important areas is insufficiently supportive of the Council's long-term goals on sustainability and zero waste, and its generalized language is too amorphous to drive policy forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: It's a lost opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: We hope the Council will play an important role, as it has in the last two solid waste management plans, in enhancing this document, and we look forward to working with you in that mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Goldstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Bronx homeowner Hannah LaShawn describes problems with containerization including theft of trash cans leading to tickets, and inability to accommodate volume spikes. She requests a theft defense for violations and ability to book large-volume pickups in advance.
chapters.title: Hannah LaShawn testifies on containerization challenges for homeowners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Hannah LaShawn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I am a homeowner in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I own a three-family where I also reside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm here today to talk about containerization, specifically two aspects that, if properly addressed by sanitation, could go a long way in supporting homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: First has to do with theft of cans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: You can't put something loose on the curb in New York City and think it's not going to get stolen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: They're going to get stolen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: Mine have been stolen multiple times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: And while I do resent having to spend time and money replacing the cans, the real insult to injury comes when, after a theft recently, I was unable to replace the can in time for my next collection day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I was then given a ticket when I put the black bag on the curb.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I went to the oath hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I explained the theft.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: They credited my testimony and found that theft was not a defense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: So I had to pay to replace the can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I had to pay for the ticket, and I had to spend time on both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm asking this committee in sanitation to work with Oath and create an official defense of theft of can would be a defense to that violation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm also asking for the ability to report the theft to sanitation so that they will not ticket me while I'm in the process of trying to replace it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: The second item that I want to talk about has to do with these momentary short-term influxes of spikes in volume.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: Normally, I'm in a small building, two cans is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: But if you've got a party, a holiday party, or you have tenants moving in and out, there might be this spike in trash.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I cannot accommodate enough cans for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: The sanitation does not allow for exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: For containerization, their suggestion is that I store extra cans on my property to use during these momentary spikes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: That's unreasonable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm already storing two black cans, two recycling, and a compost bin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm asking that this committee work with sanitation to take a policy that used to be in place for bulk collection, where you could book a bulk collection online in advance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: I'm asking that we now use that to book a large volume pickup in advance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: If I've booked it and I put my black bags on the curb, I would not be ticketed because it is with sanitation's knowledge and guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Hannah LaShawn
utterances.text: So this doesn't address everything with containerization, but these would help us.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Claire Mifflin urges DSNY to pilot shared recycling and composting bins alongside trash for residents above storefronts, calls for integrating containerization into SWAMP diversion goals, advocates for community composting expansion, and proposes a district bulk set-out day for reuse.
chapters.title: Claire Mifflin testifies on containerization pilots, community composting, and bulk set-out day

utterances.speaker: Gregory Anderson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Shravanti Kaneka of NYC EJA urges the city to deprioritize anaerobic co-digestion at wastewater facilities in favor of expanding community composting, citing unfair waste burdens on environmental justice communities and the benefits of local composting for green jobs.
chapters.title: Shravanti Kaneka (NYC Environmental Justice Alliance) testifies against anaerobic co-digestion prioritization

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: My name is Shravanti Kaneka.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Resiliency Planner with the New York City Environmental Justice Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: Founded in 1991, Nija is a nonprofit citywide membership network that links 13 grassroots organizations from low-income neighborhoods and communities of color across the five boroughs in their struggle for environmental justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: I'm here today to voice Nija's concerns about one particular aspect that was discussed about the city's approach to solid waste management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: We encourage the city to deprioritize waste management solutions like anaerobic co-digestion at city wastewater resource recovery facilities at the cost of expanding composting facilities across New York City, which could

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: help establish green job, among other numerous benefits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: As Commissioner Anderson has mentioned, 2,400 million pounds of waste are produced every day, which requires massive transportation logistics and contributes to pollution impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: as this garbage is moved by privately owned and operated waste transfer stations along the waterfront.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: DSNY data shows that the system is grossly unfair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: Just four community districts still handle 75% of the city's private waste, and the majority of this waste passes through communities with the highest asthma rates, as you mentioned, the South Bronx, North Brooklyn, and Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: Despite all of the benefits of composting, the city's composting infrastructure has not kept up with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: has not kept up pace with the collection of residential organics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: Despite successful models we've seen at Fresh Kills, we're troubled to see the continued investment in sending collected organics to be co-digested with sewage sludge at the Newtown Creek facility,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: rather than building capacity for small and mid-scale composting facilities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shravanti Kaneka
utterances.text: I know my time is nearly up, but in my written comments, I name the number of issues with anaerobic co-digestion, and I will submit more detailed testimony in writing.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Your testimony will be read.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And the first panel is relieved.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez

utterances.speaker: Ryan

utterances.speaker: Ryan

utterances.speaker: Ryan
utterances.text: The system works and works well.
